Rashi on Chagigah 21a:1:1.english: An acute mourner [onen] - [That is, one] who did not become impure through his deceased [relative].

Rashi on Chagigah 21a:1:2.hebrew: והמחוסר כפורים - כגון זב שטבל ליום שביעי לספירתו, והעריב שמשו, ולמחרת הוא קרוי מחוסר כפורים, שעדיין גמר טהרתו תלויה בקרבנו:
Rashi on Chagigah 21a:1:2.english: And one who is lacking atonement - For example, a zav who immersed on the seventh day of his count, and his sun set; on the next day he is called "lacking atonement," since the completion of his purification still depends on his offering.

Rashi on Chagigah 21a:1:3.hebrew: צריכין טבילה - לאחר שהביא קרבנו, אם רצה לאכול קדש. ובגמרא מפרש טעמא:
Rashi on Chagigah 21a:1:3.english: They require immersion - After he has brought his offering, if he wishes to eat sacred food. And the Gemara explains the reason.

Rashi on Chagigah 21a:2:1.hebrew: שכבידו של כלי חוצץ - כבידו של כלי הפנימי, המכביד על הכלי החיצון שהוא מונח בתוכו, חוצץ בפני המים, ואין טבילה עולה לא לזה ולא לזה. ולקמן (חגיגה דף כב.) פריך: אי הכי, אפילו תרומה נמי:
Rashi on Chagigah 21a:2:1.english: That the weight of a vessel causes an interposition - The weight of the inner vessel, which presses down on the outer vessel in which it is placed, forms an interposition against the water, and the immersion is effective neither for this one nor for that one. And below (Chagigah 22a) the Gemara challenges: If so, even teruma should also not be permitted:

Rashi on Chagigah 21a:3:1.hebrew: והא מדסיפא - דמעלה אחריתי דחשיב בסיפא, הוה טעמא משום חציצה, רישא לאו משום חציצה. דאי טעמא דתרוייהו משום חציצה, ולאשמעינן דגבי קדש כל דדמי לחציצה פוסל בו, ובתרומה לא פסלה אלא חציצה גמורה דאורייתא — ליתני חדא מינייהו:
Rashi on Chagigah 21a:3:1.english: But since [it is] from the latter clause - [The reasoning is that] another level that [the mishna] counts in the latter clause is for the reason of interposition, [so] the first clause is not for the reason of interposition. For if the reason of both were interposition, and [the mishna] wanted to teach us that with regard to sacred food anything resembling an interposition disqualifies it, whereas with regard to teruma only a complete interposition, [forbidden] by Torah law, disqualifies it — it should have taught only one of them.

Tosafot on Chagigah 21a:1:1.english: “An onen and one lacking atonement require immersion for sacred food, but not for teruma” - The wording “immersion” implies immersion but not nightfall (he’erev shemesh), as [the Gemara] infers below (Chagigah 23a) regarding finished vessels. So too it is implied in Zevachim, at the beginning of [the chapter] Tevul Yom (Zevachim 99a), where it asks about this Mishnah: How is this the case? If he put it out of his mind, one who was defiled by a creeping thing is fully impure. This implies that nightfall is not required. Rashi too explained so there, that nightfall is not required. And as for what we learned there: “A tevul yom and one lacking atonement do not share in the sacrificial portions, to eat in the evening”, which implies that one lacking atonement does require nightfall — one can say that [the Mishnah] mentioned him because of the tevul yom. But this is difficult for Rabbeinu Yitzchak, who said, in Eruvin in the chapter Bechol Me’arvin (Eruvin 32a): “A woman who has a [pending] birth or zivah [offering] brings money and puts it in the shofar-chest, immerses, and eats sacrificial food in the evening”, and there it does not teach tevul yom. And one can answer that the “evening” mentioned there speaks of one who is not standing there at the time of the offering, but relies on the presumption of the court, and eats in the evening, for the presumption is that the court is not lazy. But it is difficult: [if so,] it should be permitted after midday, since we found regarding the omer (Menachot 68a) that those far away are permitted from midday onward, because the court is not lazy. And one can distinguish: there, with a public offering, they hurry more to do it by midday, whereas a private offering they wait for all day, but no longer, lest he stumble through them. And if you say, “After the afternoon tamid it should be permitted,” [the answer is that] it should no longer be permitted, since “the olah” is written about it, and from it we derive the positive commandment of completion, that nothing is offered after the olah of the tamid at twilight. But one can say that sometimes they delayed the tamid until nightfall, as we say at the beginning of [the chapter] Tefillat HaShachar (Berakhot 26b), that it goes on being offered until the evening. Therefore, since it has no fixed time, they are in doubt about her in every possible doubt. Or alternatively, [it follows] Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who said at the beginning of [the chapter] Tamid Nishchat (Pesachim 59a) that the bird sin offering is offered after the evening tamid. And so Rabbeinu Yitzchak explains at the beginning of Tamid Nishchat, regarding one lacking atonement who immerses and eats sacrificial food in the evening: it does not mention “evening” because of nightfall, but because he does not stand by his offering the whole time, as I explained, and relies on the presumption of the priests. And so one can explain that [passage] in Keritot at the beginning of the chapter Mechusrei Kapara (Keritot 8b): [A convert] is barred from eating sacrificial food until he brings [his offering]; if he brought one pigeon in the morning, he eats sacrificial food in the evening. It mentions a novelty; for even though, if he brought both in the morning, he would not eat until evening, where he relies on the presumption, as I explained. But one cannot say there that it is because of nightfall, since it is not needed, as I explained; and further, it does not mention immersion there; and we have not found anyone lacking atonement who requires immersion except one lacking atonement for impurity, but for a convert we have not found it. And so we learned (Parah 11:5): “Anyone who requires immersion by rabbinic decree defiles sacred things, etc.; after his immersion he is permitted for all of them.” This implies that whatever is rabbinic is permitted immediately, without nightfall. And from that [Mishnah] which I mentioned, Rabbi Shmuel of Ras derived an answer to what is taught in the second chapter of Beitzah (18a) regarding the Mishnah of a vessel that became impure with an offspring of impurity — that one may immerse it on a festival. Why? It requires nightfall! And he answered: since an offspring of impurity is rabbinic, it does not require nightfall. And so it is implied in the Yerushalmi, Terumot chapter 2, in the Gemara: “One who immerses his vessels on Shabbat — is he fixing a vessel? Initially? It was taught: if his vessels fell into a pit, he contrives and immerses it,” that is, on a festival and on Shabbat. Two Amoraim [disagree]: one said it refers to a vessel that became impure with a primary source of impurity (av hatumah), and one said with an offspring of impurity. The one who said offspring objects to the one who said primary source: even on a weekday it requires nightfall! That is, it is fine for me, who established it as an offspring of impurity, for it does not require nightfall; but for you, who establish it as a primary source of impurity, it requires nightfall and is not fit to be used except on a weekday, so it would be immersing from Shabbat for the weekday. And he establishes it as one who wants to use it for unconsecrated food, since a tevul yom is permitted for unconsecrated food without nightfall. And now, according to his words, they establish the Mishnah of Beitzah (there), that one may not immerse vessels that became impure with a primary source of impurity, as speaking of a priest who is to eat teruma, or one who eats unconsecrated food in the purity of teruma; and rabbinic impurity is permitted only through a contrivance. Also the discussions of Beitzah speak of a contrivance, whereas with a primary source of impurity, not even through a contrivance. And as for what the Mishnah there permits — to draw water with an impure bucket, which becomes pure by itself — this contrivance is better than returning it empty. And that text is well cited in the Yerushalmi; also in the second chapter of Beitzah it is written erroneously in the books; but my presentation of the text is as I explained. And Rabbeinu Yitzchak further brought a support from what is said in the chapter HaIshah (Pesachim 90b): Rav said: One does not slaughter and sprinkle for one defiled by a creeping thing, lest he be negligent and not immerse. But regarding one lacking atonement he said there that we slaughter and sprinkle for him and are not concerned lest he be negligent, since he is fully pure by Torah law; the Sages did not uphold their words against [a transgression punishable by] karet, to exempt him thereby from the Pesach offering, and so we properly slaughter and sprinkle for him. And do not be surprised, for it says in the chapter Hotzi’u Lo (Yoma 47a) regarding Rabbi Yishmael ben Kimchit, the High Priest who spoke with a gentile in the marketplace and a spray of spittle came from his mouth: his brother Yeshevav entered and served in his place. But why? Let him go immerse! Since the impurity is rabbinic, it does not require nightfall. There one can say that since the Sages made gentiles like zavim for all their purposes, they were stringent regarding them and required nightfall. And regarding the spittle of an am ha’aretz, it is implied later (Chagigah 23a), in that case of the tube, that nightfall is required, where it says: Why should he become impure and immerse? He is already impure and standing! What is it saying? [That] with the first impurity, nightfall is not required and there is no recognizable difference; but if they defile him, nightfall is required, and there is properly a recognizable difference for the Sadducees. Rather, surely even that of an am ha’aretz requires nightfall. Furthermore, we learned (Parah 3:7) that they would defile the priest who burns the [red] heifer, and it is taught in the Tosefta that they would touch him, as [Tosafot] explained earlier, that the garments of those who eat sacred food are midras for a sin offering. What recognizable difference for the Sadducees would there be, if nightfall were not required, as I said? Rabbi Shimon answered that they made him like one impure from a corpse on his seventh day, as above; therefore nightfall too is required. But Rashi did not explain so later; rather, he explained that they made him like one impure from a corpse on his seventh day, to count in him first and second [degrees of impurity], and not with regard to nightfall. And now it is difficult, since it implies that there is nightfall even with rabbinic impurity, whereas in that [Mishnah] “Anyone who requires immersion” it implies that there is no nightfall. And Rabbeinu Yitzchak said that [the Mishnah] about defiling the priest who burns the heifer speaks of doing so in order that he be impure enough to defile unconsecrated food by his touch; and so too in that case [of the spittle of an am ha’aretz and of the gentile] that defiles unconsecrated food by touch; therefore they required nightfall. But the wording does not imply that he defiles unconsecrated food by touch in the case of the priest who burns the heifer; and likewise later, regarding the tube, it says “they made him like one impure from a corpse on his seventh day” only with regard to nightfall, and not with regard to defiling unconsecrated food by touch. And as for the fact that nightfall is required, one can say that regarding the heifer they were stringent, and also in the case of the tube, more than with finished vessels, for which immersion without nightfall suffices — that is, regarding unconsecrated food and teruma, and for sacred food, but not for a sin offering. And as for that [passage] in Pesachim, chapter Eilu Devarim (Pesachim 70a), which says: A knife found on the thirteenth, he studies and immerses it on the fourteenth, and slaughters with it immediately — that is, presumably they immersed it the day before, in order to account for nightfall. And if you say, let us be concerned lest it became impure with a rabbinic impurity that does not require nightfall, and he kept it until morning to immerse it — [that is] a rabbinic doubt, and [we rule] leniently; and furthermore, it is customary to immerse in the evening, lest he be so preoccupied that he does not immerse. And one cannot raise the question of where this knife was found: if in Jerusalem, even on the thirteenth also; and if outside Jerusalem, even on the fourteenth not so, as we say there at the end of the first chapter of Pesachim (19b). For one can say that it speaks of outside Jerusalem; or alternatively in Jerusalem, in a gazita that is neither on the way down nor on the way up; and on the fourteenth there is evidence that it was immersed, so it is permitted. And Rabbi Eliyahu asked: Let us disqualify this knife through diverted attention (hesech hada’at), as is said earlier at the end of the second chapter (20a), where he said, “My mind was on the basket and not on the hoe,” and we disqualified it through diverted attention. And Rabbeinu Yitzchak answered that diverted attention applies to disqualify only like there, where it was in his hand and he diverted his attention from it; but where it is not in his hand, such as when it was lost, diverted attention does not apply there to disqualify. And Rabbi Elchanan brought support for his words from [the chapter] 7 of Shekalim (Mishnah 3), which says there: If limbs are found in the Temple courtyard, [they are] olah; pieces, [they are] sin offerings. This implies that an olah is offered and a sin offering is eaten, and it is not disqualified through diverted attention. And Rabbi Elchanan asked: What is this wording, “teaches and immerses,” which implies that it was already immersed? And Rabbeinu Yitzchak answered him: even if it was recognized that its owners had immersed it, they immerse it again, for say it was not guarded in purity, since he has the whole day. And regarding that [Mishnah] of Beitzah, where we say that a vessel that became impure with an offspring of impurity may be immersed, and we ask, “But it requires nightfall!”, Rabbi Elchanan used to say that we are dealing with a festival that falls on Friday, since a festival prepares for Shabbat, so they immerse even for the next day. But the wording of the Mishnah does not imply this to him; rather, it speaks of any festival:
